items.title: Bitcoin Core discloses three flaws it fixed last year
items.what: On 10 November, Bitcoin Core developers published details of three vulnerabilities, fixed in releases from October 2025, after support for the 29.x versions ended on 27 October. The most serious, rated high, could stop affected miners' nodes from building new blocks after a chain reorganisation until they were restarted. The two medium-rated issues could delay block processing or wrongly give Tor peers trusted status on nodes using a non-default setting. Reporting on the disclosures says none allowed theft of bitcoin or creation of coins, and no exploitation was reported.
items.why: Bitcoin's software is reviewed in the open, and flaws are usually fixed quietly first and disclosed once older versions are retired. Anyone who runs their own node or wallet software benefits from keeping it on a maintained version.

items.title: Draft proposals to stop a hardware wallet leaking its seed
items.what: The Bitcoin Optech newsletter of 13 November reported two draft Bitcoin Improvement Proposals for "anti-exfil" signing. The idea is that the computer or phone adds its own randomness to each signature a hardware wallet makes, so a tampered device cannot hide pieces of its seed in the signatures it produces. The drafts include test code; their author notes the cryptography has not yet been audited and asks for review.
items.why: A hardware wallet is trusted to keep keys secret, and this work aims to reduce how much trust a single device needs. Where a device comes from, and keeping a verified backup of the seed, remain the foundations.

items.title: US Treasury reported to be drafting custody rules for government bitcoin
items.what: On 13 November, Crypto Briefing reported that the US Treasury is drafting a framework for holding the government's bitcoin, combining keys held by the government with third-party custodians. The holdings come mainly from seizures and are kept in the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve set up by executive order in March 2025; estimates of their size vary depending on which coins tied up in court cases are counted. No official announcement has been published, and whether to disclose the holdings publicly is reported to be still under discussion.
items.why: Even a government has to decide who controls the keys, how many parties are involved and what happens if one fails. The same questions apply, at a smaller scale, to any long-term holder.

items.title: Mining difficulty falls about 9% as computing power leaves the network
items.what: At block 975,744, reached on 13–14 November, Bitcoin's mining difficulty adjusted down by about 9.1%. In the preceding two weeks, blocks had been arriving every 10.7 minutes or so on average instead of the 10-minute target, as some miners switched machines off or redirected power to other uses. The adjustment makes finding a block easier for the miners that remain.
items.why: This is the difficulty adjustment doing its job: every 2,016 blocks the network rebalances itself so blocks keep arriving at a steady pace, whoever is mining. No one decides it; it is part of the rules.

items.title: Binance says it has fully replaced the assets taken in October's hack
items.what: On 12 November, Binance said it had completed coverage of all assets affected by the 29 October theft, using its user protection fund, its futures insurance fund and company money, and that it will rebuild the user fund to about $1 billion. It published a new proof-of-reserves snapshot, with the cryptographic proof that lets customers check their balances still to follow. US audit regulators have warned that proof-of-reserves reports are not audits.
items.why: Customers were made whole this time because the platform chose to, and could afford to. A reserve snapshot shows assets at one moment, not a company's debts or controls, so it is one input among several when judging a custodian.

items.title: Binance explains how the record hack began: a fake job interview
items.what: On 3 November, Binance published its account of the 29 October theft. In September, an engineer looking for a new job downloaded a malicious code repository after a fake interview with a fictitious company; earlier, in June, another employee had installed a tampered tool found through a search advert. The attackers used these footholds to take over wallet developers' machines and trigger the transfers. Binance says it is repaying all affected customers.
items.why: The largest exchange was breached through ordinary people, not through Bitcoin itself. The same tactics, fake job offers, fake software and fake adverts, are used against individual holders and their devices.
items.learn: Hacks: when a platform or a device is attacked

items.title: US Treasury cuts exchange MEXC off from the US financial system
items.what: On 6 November, the US Treasury's financial crimes unit, FinCEN, issued an order barring US financial institutions from moving funds to or from MEXC Global. Treasury alleges the exchange handled at least $16 billion in illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, linked to Iran, North Korea and Russian sanctions evasion. The order takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register. MEXC had not publicly responded at the time of reporting.
items.why: An exchange can lose its banking links through regulatory action, which can make deposits and withdrawals in money difficult at short notice. A platform's licences and compliance record are part of its risk, alongside its security.

items.title: Listed miners turn their sites over to AI data centres
items.what: Quarterly results this week showed large listed miners shifting from Bitcoin mining to leasing power and buildings to AI companies. On 4 November, Riot Platforms reported a 15-year lease of its entire Corsicana campus in Texas to an AI lab and said it has sold 20,264 BTC this year, mainly to fund data centre building. On 2 November, Cipher Digital reported mining revenue down 63% as its first data centre lease began.
items.why: Mining secures the network, and the companies doing it change as business conditions change. The rules and the difficulty adjustment are designed so that the network keeps working whoever mines, but mining is becoming a smaller part of some well-known firms.

items.title: Tether says it holds about 150,000 BTC, more than its report shows
items.what: On 3 November, at the Plan ₿ Forum in Lugano, Tether's chief executive said the company holds "give or take 150,000 bitcoin". Its third-quarter reserve report, which covers the assets backing its USDT stablecoin, implies about 100,000 BTC. Tether says its own company holdings are kept separate from those reserves; where the remaining coins are held was not disclosed.
items.why: Large holders are often judged by what they say, not what they publish. Statements are not the same as audited figures, and how a company reports its holdings is part of judging it.

items.title: Binance hit by the largest crypto theft on record
items.what: On 29 October, attackers took about $6.4 billion from Binance hot wallets on around ten blockchains in roughly 20 minutes, including about 18,270 BTC. Blockchain analytics firms and the FBI attribute the attack to a North Korean group. Binance suspended withdrawals, says it will absorb the losses rather than its users, and began reopening withdrawals on 1 November.
items.why: Coins held on a platform are a claim on that platform. Even the largest exchange can pause withdrawals for days. Where your keys sit, and what you would do during such a pause, is part of your plan.

items.title: Quantum risk moves from research papers to boardrooms
items.what: On 30 October, the board of a Nasdaq-listed company approved a plan to sell or pledge its 5,833 BTC, citing the Binance hack and quantum computing risk. Research published this year lowered the estimated machine size needed to break Bitcoin's signatures about 20-fold, although today's machines remain far from it. BIP-360, a proposal for a quantum-resistant address type, is in Bitcoin's proposal repository with no activation date.
items.why: The risk concerns coins whose public key is already visible on the blockchain, mainly old and reused addresses. It is a long-term protocol topic, debated openly. Avoiding address reuse is a habit you control today.

items.title: Strategy reports its quarter: 848,517 BTC on the balance sheet
items.what: On 29 October, Strategy, the largest listed holder of Bitcoin, reported third-quarter results driven by the change in value of its holdings, and announced that its CFO is leaving on 5 November.
items.why: Under fair-value accounting, the profits of Bitcoin treasury companies swing with the Bitcoin price, in both directions. A share in such a company is exposure to the company, its debt and its decisions, not Bitcoin itself.
